newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Dec 30.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Dec 30.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
-- WATER COMPETITION PLAN AXED

Government plans for a national grid for water and greater competition across the water industry have been abandoned amid doubts as to the technical feasibility and potential consumer benefits of the scheme. The proposals to introduce wholesale competition across the industry were introduced in 1995, but are now likely to be dropped before the general election.
-- LABOUR DITCHES PLANS TO RE-REGULATE BUSES

The Labour party has abandoned plans for a Labour government to re-regulate Britain's bus industry. Shadow transport secretary Andrew Smith is to issue a consultation paper early next year outlining Labour's approach to bus regulation, which is expected to be a regime designed to improve the quality of services, rather than the bureaucratic and anti-competitive plans for wholesale re-regulation.
-- FIRST QUARTER JOB PROSPECTS RISE

A survey from the independent employment agency Manpower has claimed that first quarter job prospects for Britain in 1997 will be the best for seven years. The survey found that up to 26 per cent of employers in manufacturing expect a net increase in job prospects in the period, and 40 per cent of employers in the telecommunications sector expect an increase in jobs.
Regionally, Manpower found that the south of England has replaced the east Midlands as the most confident region in the UK for jobs.
-- FOREIGN CAPITAL STATISTICS A 'DECEIT'

The Labour party has published figures which show that 60 per cent of inward investment in the UK in 1995 was due to takeovers of British companies by overseas firms. Stephen Byers, the party's shadow employment minister, used the figures to charge that the government has been misleading people in its claims over inward investment. Byers said that Britain's assets are being sold abroad with profits syphoned off overseas, and the government applauds this as inward investment.
-- BUSINESSES SEEK REFORM OF ANNUAL REPORT

The Hempel Committee, the body headed by ICI chairman Sir Ronnie Hempel which is reviewing the code of boardroom conduct set out by the Cadbury Committee, is to be urged to promote new ways for companies to communicate with their stakeholders. The call comes from the Centre for Tomorrow's Company, an influential group of companies which has set up a taskforce with the Institute of Public Relations to look at reforming the annual report.
-- US EQUITIES BOOST EUROPEAN GROUPS

Figures from Wall Street research firm Securities Data show that European companies raised $6.1 billion in new capital on US equity markets in 1996. In an outstanding year for new issuance on US markets, 38 European companies issued shares for the first time. The largest non-US offering of the year was the sale by the German government of a large stake in national telecommunications company Deutsche Telekom, which raised $1.6 billion on the US market.
-- NEW HANSON PLANS US EXPANSION

New Hanson, one of the companies formed by the demerger of the Hanson group, is targeting expansion in the US as the key to growth in its core buildings business following the split. Meanwhile Energy Group, the last Hanson company to be spun off, has agreed a deal with its banks clearing up to 700 million stg for acquisitions, mainly in the US. The Energy Group has an interest in eight power stations in the UK as well as the Peabody coal mining business in the US.
-- VOLVO AND MITSUBISHI TO DISCUSS TRUCK-MAKING LINK

Swedish vehicle giant Volvo is to hold talks in the new year with Japan's Mitsubishi over ways to co-operate in truck-making operations in Europe and Asia. The two companies already jointly operate a car plant in the Netherlands, but Mitsubishi is keen to expand its truck business in Europe while Volvo wants to extend its penetration in the Asian markets for trucks.
-- CABLE INDUSTRY SEEKS TALKS

The UK's cable companies, which earlier this year failed in a bid to persuade the Office of Fair Trading that BSkyB had abused its dominant position in the provision of specialist television channels, are seeking talks with the satellite broadcaster early in the new year. The largest cable companies want to persuade BSkyB to offer them 'fairer' terms of trade.
-- ISRAELI GROUP SEES UK LAUNCH OF MS DRUG

Israeli drugs company Teva Pharmaceuticals is looking to UK regulatory approval for one of its products as a gateway to other European markets. Teva has said it expects to gain UK approval for its Copaxone treatment for multiple sclerosis sometime in 1997, and that UK approval will allow the drug access to European markets via the mutual recognition procedure.
